title: Why Is Your WooCommerce B2B Store Slow? A 60-Second Diagnostic and Fix Guide

linkedin.post:
Your lead buyer waits six seconds for the catalog to load, and you're holding a $150K replatforming quote.

Before you sign, run a diagnostic. In many cases like this, the culprit is a Redis configuration that takes an afternoon to fix.

Generic WooCommerce speed advice is written for B2C stores. It assumes anonymous visitors and safe full-page caching. B2B buyers break both assumptions.

Logged-in buyers bypass the page cache. Every page is built fresh because pricing is tiered per customer.

Here is where the slowness usually hides:

- Server defaults that were never tuned, like the InnoDB buffer pool and PHP-FPM
- Redis object caching that is missing or not scoped per user
- Slow admin order lookups that need HPOS enabled
- ERP sync firing on WordPress hooks during page loads

The article starts with a 60-second self-audit. Match your symptom to a bottleneck, then go straight to that fix.

It also covers when a replatform is the right call. That is a capability gap, such as multi-company approval workflows or native quote management. It is not a speed problem.

slides.headline: Your slow store may not need a new platform
slides.sub: Run a 60-second diagnostic before you sign a $150K replatform quote.
slides.alt: Cover slide: a slow WooCommerce B2B store may not need a new platform

slides.headline: B2B buyers bypass the page cache
slides.body: Logged-in buyers get pages built fresh because pricing is tiered per customer. Full-page caching gives them nothing.
slides.alt: Point 1: logged-in B2B buyers bypass full-page caching

slides.headline: Use Redis object caching, scoped per user
slides.body: Cache expensive queries like pricing and visibility checks, not whole pages. Scope pricing per user so it never bleeds across sessions.
slides.alt: Point 2: Redis object caching scoped per user fixes B2B caching

slides.headline: Enable HPOS for slow admin orders
slides.body: Order lookups taking 10-30 seconds point to HPOS or Action Scheduler bloat. Test the migration on staging first.
slides.alt: Point 3: slow admin order lookups point to HPOS and Action Scheduler

slides.headline: Tune the server defaults
slides.body: The InnoDB buffer pool default is 128MB. Left alone, MySQL reads from disk on most queries of a large store.
slides.alt: Point 4: untuned MySQL and PHP defaults slow every page

slides.headline: Move ERP sync off page loads
slides.body: Sync on WordPress hooks adds ERP calls to customer requests. Switch to scheduled batch sync every 5-15 minutes.
slides.alt: Point 5: batch ERP sync removes latency from customer pages

slides.headline: Replatform for gaps, not speed
slides.body: Multi-company approval workflows or native quotes are real reasons. Slowness alone is not.
slides.alt: Point 6: replatform only for capability gaps, not for speed
